events.title: Potosí silver and the mita labour draft
hints: A mountain of silver financed an empire and consumed the lives of conscripted miners.
A rotating labour draft inherited from an earlier empire sent men to the mines.
events.summary: After silver was found at Cerro Rico in 1545, Potosí became one of the world's largest cities. Spain used the mita, a rotating labour draft adapted from Inca practice, to supply miners, and the silver shaped the global economy until independence.

events.title: War of the Pacific and the loss of the coast
hints: A dispute over a tax on nitrate exports ended with the loss of all ocean access.
It has been landlocked ever since.
events.summary: A dispute over taxes on Chilean nitrate companies in Antofagasta led to the War of the Pacific. Chile occupied the Bolivian coastal province and kept it under the 1884 truce, leaving Bolivia without a coastline.

events.title: Inca conquest of the Titicaca basin
hints: Emperors based far to the north absorbed the powerful kingdoms around a great high-altitude lake in the 15th century.
The conquered Aymara-speaking lords were bound to provide labour service known as mit'a.
Their lands formed the southern quarter of the empire, called Collasuyu.
events.summary: In the 15th century the Inca rulers Pachacuti and Túpac Yupanqui conquered the Aymara kingdoms around Lake Titicaca and the high plateau. The region became part of Collasuyu, the southern quarter of the empire, and communities supplied labour and tribute until the Spanish arrived in 1532.

events.title: Acre War and the rubber territory
hints: A remote western rainforest region booming with rubber was settled mostly by migrants from a bigger neighbour in the 1890s.
A short war and a local republic ended with the loss of the territory.
The 1903 Treaty of Petrópolis ceded about 190,000 square kilometres in exchange for money and a railway promise.
events.summary: Brazilian rubber tappers poured into the Acre region, then Bolivian territory, from the 1870s. Revolts and a short-lived Independent State of Acre led to the 1903 Treaty of Petrópolis, by which Bolivia ceded about 190,000 square kilometres for £2 million and a promised railway.
